title: "State of health in BC: a descriptive report"

::: {.callout-note}
## Version and observation window

**Report version 0.1** · observation windows: mortality **1991–2024**,
life expectancy **1980–2024** · generated from the published datasets by
`quarto render`. Regenerate the underlying data with
`uv run sohbc build` before re-rendering (see [Reproduce](#reproduce)).

Numbers in this report are **regenerated on every build** from the files
under `data/published/`; nothing here is typed in by hand. If a figure and
this prose disagree, the figure is right.
:::

This is the first edition of the project's "State of health in BC"
descriptive report (deliverable of milestone M3 in the
[roadmap](../ROADMAP.md)). It describes what the currently-ingested
indicators show — **not** the state of health in full. Two indicators are
published so far, both in the mortality domain; the report will widen as
the indicator set does, and each edition carries its observation window
because the numbers are dated, not timeless
([why](../explanation/nonstationarity.qmd)).

## What is covered

| Indicator | Domain | Window | Resolution | Sexes | Source |
|-----------|--------|--------|------------|-------|--------|
| [Mortality rates](indicator-mortality-rates-bc.qmd) | Mortality | 1991–2024 | provincial | both, M, F | StatCan 13-10-0710-01 |
| [Life expectancy at birth](indicator-life-expectancy-bc.qmd) | Mortality | 1980–2024 | provincial | both, M, F | StatCan 13-10-0837-01 |

Both are **proxies** for the mortality domain, not the state of health
itself, and both are at provincial resolution — sub-provincial
inequalities are not yet described (see [Next editions](#next-editions)).

## The headline: every series moves, and the rules change

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
mort = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc_trend.json").json()
mortAsr = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc_age_standardised_trend.json").json()
life = FileAttachment("../data/published/life_expectancy_bc_trend.json").json()
lifeBySex = FileAttachment("../data/published/life_expectancy_bc_by_sex_trend.json").json()
mortBySex = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc_by_sex_trend.json").json()

summary = [
  {series: "Mortality rate (crude)", window: `${mort.start}–${mort.end}`, slope_per_decade: mort.overall.slope_per_decade, verdict: mort.stationarity.verdict, breaks: mort.change_points.join(", ") || "—"},
  {series: "Mortality rate (age-standardised)", window: `${mortAsr.start}–${mortAsr.end}`, slope_per_decade: mortAsr.overall.slope_per_decade, verdict: mortAsr.stationarity.verdict, breaks: mortAsr.change_points.join(", ") || "—"},
  {series: "Life expectancy at birth", window: `${life.start}–${life.end}`, slope_per_decade: life.overall.slope_per_decade, verdict: life.stationarity.verdict, breaks: life.change_points.join(", ") || "—"}
]
Inputs.table(summary, {
  columns: ["series", "window", "slope_per_decade", "verdict", "breaks"],
  header: {series: "series", window: "window", slope_per_decade: "slope/decade", verdict: "stationarity", breaks: "regime breaks"}
})
```

Three things follow from the table, and they are the report's core
finding:

1. **Nothing is stationary.** Every series changes over its window; a
   single summary value would be false to all of them.
2. **Direction differs by measure.** The crude mortality rate and life
   expectancy trend in opposite senses, because crude mortality is not
   age-adjusted while life expectancy already integrates the age pattern
   of death.
3. **The change is not one slope.** Every series carries at least one
   regime break beyond a straight line (all significant at the 5% level
   by the residual-permutation test); the breaks are the story, not noise.

## Mortality: an ageing population masks a turning point

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
rows = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc.csv").csv({typed: true})
rates = rows.filter(d => d.characteristic === "Mortality rate per 1,000 population" && d.age_group === "Age at time of death, all ages" && d.sex === "Both sexes")
asr = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc_age_standardised.csv").csv({typed: true}).filter(d => d.sex === "Both sexes")
series = rates.map(d => ({year: d.ref_date, rate: d.value, series: "Crude"}))
  .concat(asr.map(d => ({year: d.ref_date, rate: d.value, series: "Age-standardised"})))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  title: "Mortality rate, British Columbia (per 1,000 population)",
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d"},
  y: {grid: true, label: "Deaths per 1,000 population"},
  color: {legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectX([{x1: 2020, x2: 2024}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", fill: "grey", fillOpacity: 0.12}),
    Plot.ruleX(mort.change_points, {stroke: "red", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.ruleX(mortAsr.change_points, {stroke: "steelblue", strokeDasharray: "2,3"}),
    Plot.lineY(series, {x: "year", y: "rate", stroke: "series", tip: true}),
    Plot.dot(series, {x: "year", y: "rate", stroke: "series", tip: true})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Over ${mort.start}–${mort.end} the **crude** rate rose by
**${mort.overall.slope_per_decade.toFixed(2)}** per 1,000 per decade, while the
**age-standardised** rate, which removes the effect of population ageing,
changed by **${mortAsr.overall.slope_per_decade.toFixed(2)}** — i.e. it *fell*
on net. The crude rise is largely the ageing of the population, not a
worsening of age-specific risk. The age-standardised series is the one that
abstracts from that: it declined from 1991 and its regime turned at
**${mortAsr.change_point}**, after which the decline flattened and
reversed. The pink band marks the COVID-19 period (2020–2024).`
```

The gap between the two lines is the signature of demographic ageing, and
it is exactly why the project reports both and treats the standardised
series as the one about risk rather than the one about the age structure.

## Life expectancy: two decades of gain, then a stall

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
lifeRows = FileAttachment("../data/published/life_expectancy_bc.csv").csv({typed: true}).filter(d => d.characteristic === "Life expectancy (in years) at age x (ex)" && d.age_group === "0 years" && d.sex !== "Both sexes")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  title: "Life expectancy at birth by sex, British Columbia (years)",
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d"},
  y: {grid: true, label: "Years", domain: [70, 90]},
  color: {legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectX([{x1: 2020, x2: 2024}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", fill: "grey", fillOpacity: 0.12}),
    Plot.ruleX(lifeBySex.levels.Males.change_points, {stroke: "red", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.ruleX(lifeBySex.levels.Females.change_points, {stroke: "steelblue", strokeDasharray: "2,3"}),
    Plot.lineY(lifeRows, {x: "ref_date", y: "value", stroke: "sex", tip: true}),
    Plot.dot(lifeRows, {x: "ref_date", y: "value", stroke: "sex", tip: true})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Life expectancy at birth (both sexes) rose by
**${life.overall.slope_per_decade.toFixed(2)}** years per decade on average
across ${life.start}–${life.end}, but as two regimes: gains of about
**${life.segments[0].slope_per_decade.toFixed(2)}** years per decade to
**${life.change_point}**, then a flat-to-declining
**${life.segments[1].slope_per_decade.toFixed(2)}** years per decade after.
The post-2015 stall spans the COVID-19 period, which is visible as the
2020–2022 dip, but the regime turn **precedes** the pandemic — the pipeline
dates the change and does not attribute it.`
```

This is the project's nonstationarity claim in one series: the same
indicator, the same source, but a different rule before and after 2015.
The male and female series turn differently (below), so even this
agreement about *whether* there was a break comes with disagreement about
*when*.

## Sex differences

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sexRows = ["Males", "Females"].flatMap(sex => [
  {indicator: "Life expectancy", sex, ...lifeBySex.levels[sex]},
  {indicator: "Mortality (crude)", sex, ...mortBySex.crude[sex]},
  {indicator: "Mortality (age-standardised)", sex, ...mortBySex.age_standardised[sex]}
]).map(d => ({
  indicator: d.indicator,
  sex: d.sex,
  window: `${d.start}–${d.end}`,
  slope_per_decade: d.overall.slope_per_decade,
  verdict: d.stationarity.verdict,
  breaks: d.change_points.join(", ") || "—"
}))
Inputs.table(sexRows, {
  columns: ["indicator", "sex", "window", "slope_per_decade", "verdict", "breaks"],
  header: {indicator: "indicator", sex: "sex", window: "window", slope_per_decade: "slope/decade", verdict: "stationarity", breaks: "regime breaks"}
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
lifeFull = FileAttachment("../data/published/life_expectancy_bc.csv").csv({typed: true})
finalYear = String(lifeBySex.levels.Females.end)
finalFemale = lifeFull.find(d => d.ref_date === finalYear && d.age_group === "0 years" && d.sex === "Females" && d.characteristic === "Life expectancy (in years) at age x (ex)").value
finalMale = lifeFull.find(d => d.ref_date === finalYear && d.age_group === "0 years" && d.sex === "Males" && d.characteristic === "Life expectancy (in years) at age x (ex)").value
md`In ${finalYear}, life expectancy at birth was **${finalFemale.toFixed(1)}**
years for females versus **${finalMale.toFixed(1)}** for males, a gap of
about ${(finalFemale - finalMale).toFixed(1)} years. Both sexes moved in
regimes rather than one straight line: the male series turns at
**${lifeBySex.levels.Males.change_point}** and the female at
**${lifeBySex.levels.Females.change_point}**, so a single both-sexes
trajectory would blur two differently-timed changes. On the
age-standardised mortality series the male decline-then-reversal is
steeper than the female (males' regime breaks at
${mortBySex.age_standardised.Males.change_point}, females' at
${mortBySex.age_standardised.Females.change_point}).`
```

## Inequalities across regions

**Not yet described.** Both current indicators are published at
*provincial* resolution only. The road map's M3 calls for inequality
reporting across health authorities and regions; that requires
sub-provincial ingestion (separate Statistics Canada health-region tables,
or BC-specific sources such as BCCDC's dashboards), which is outstanding.
Until then this report makes **no claim about regional inequality** —
treat any provincial average here as one that could sit atop very
different regional trajectories.

## Reading this report

- **Dates are the point.** Every number above belongs to its window;
  reproducing the pipeline on refreshed data may change the verdicts.
- **Two proxies, one domain.** Mortality and life expectancy are both
  mortality-domain proxies. Nothing here speaks to morbidity, mental
  health, functional status, or wellbeing.
- **Break detection is not explanation.** The dated regimes come from a
  formal test of departure from a straight line
  [@truong2020selective]; the test says *where* the rule changes, not
  *why*. Attribution is M4/M5 work.
- **Aggregates hide sub-series.** A both-sexes series is not a summary of
  the male and female trajectories; read them separately.

## Reproduce

```bash
uv run sohbc fetch statcan_wds statcan_life_tables
uv run sohbc build
quarto render reference/state-of-health-report.qmd
```

The report reads only the files under `data/published/`, so it regenerates
end-to-end from raw data with the commands above — the acceptance
criterion of milestone M3.

## Next editions

Planned (M3 outstanding work):

- the wider indicator set (morbidity, mental health, functional status,
  wellbeing, subjective wellbeing);
- sub-provincial (health-authority / HSDA) map and inequality views;
- age-specific trajectories, not only all-ages;
- explicit regime-aware within-versus-across-regime comparisons.
